extracted.intended_audience: writers, readers, and researchers interested in the flash fiction/microfiction genre (including contest entrants and journal submitters)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the flash fiction (very short story) form: its defining features, commonly used word-count categories, and publication/contest constraints. Useful for authors composing or submitting microfiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity with character and plot development
rubrics_metrics.description: Flash fiction is a brief fictional narrative that still offers character and plot development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite extreme brevity, a flash piece should contain discernible elements of character and some form of plot or narrative movement; the form emphasizes delivering those elements within a very small word/space budget.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to hint at or imply a larger story
rubrics_metrics.description: Flash fiction possesses a unique literary quality in its ability to hint at or imply a larger story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong flash often suggests events beyond the text, leaving implication or resonance that points to a fuller narrative context. The page cites commentators who view this implication as central to the form's literary value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varieties defined by strict word/character counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Varieties are sometimes defined by word count, including the six-word story, the 280-character story ('twitterature'), the 'dribble'/'minisaga' (50 words), and the 'drabble'/'microfiction' (100 words).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different named subforms carry conventional maximums and expectations; when writing to a named subform, adhere to its customary limit and the succinctness that limit implies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to publication/contest limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Contests and journals often set concrete maximum word counts (example: Jerome Stern's contest originally <250 words; later increased to 500 words by the hosting journal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When submitting, follow the specific word-count limits of the venue (many flash journals and contests enforce strict maxima). Historical examples illustrate that accepted limits vary by venue and over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of language — 'every word counts'
rubrics_metrics.description: Flash fiction requires extreme economy: every word must contribute to meaning and effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting on flash contests and commentary emphasizes that spare, purposeful wording is a practical and aesthetic requirement; avoid filler or unnecessary exposition because of tight length constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone/energy: intensity, urgency, and impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Flash fiction is often characterized as 'intense, urgent and a little explosive.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many practitioners and critics value a concentrated emotional or rhetorical impact in flash pieces — compressed narrative energy that produces a strong reader reaction in few words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form/medium influences style and constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Platform and medium (print anthologies, online journals, Twitter/280-character formats) shape flash fiction's form and style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rise of online journals and social-media formats has influenced flash's popularity and stylistic tendencies; writers should consider the affordances and limits of the intended publication medium when composing (e.g., character limits, display format).

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexible boundaries of the form
rubrics_metrics.description: The borders of flash fiction are flexible rather than rigidly fixed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While word-count categories and named subforms exist, editors and anthologies treat the form with varying tolerances and definitions (the term 'flash fiction' itself came into use relatively recently), so be aware that expectations can differ across venues and over time.
